newsitem.title: USA: Hoffenberg loses bid to drop guilty plea.
newsitem.headline: Hoffenberg loses bid to drop guilty plea.

text.p: Steven Hoffenberg, accused of masterminding one of the biggest financial swindles in history, failed to convince a judge Tuesday that he was mentally ill when he pleaded guilty to securities fraud last year.

U.S. District Judge Robert Sweet refused to throw out the April 1995 plea by Hoffenberg, who headed the scandal-ridden Towers Financial Corp., after finding there was no evidence to support the defendant's claim.

"On the contrary, the record refutes any such contention and establishes that Hoffenberg's plea was entered into voluntarily, with a full understanding of the nature of the charges and the consequences of the plea," Sweet wrote.

The judge cited a psychologist's conclusion that Hoffenberg's present description of his mental state at the time of the plea was highly suspect because tests showed that "Hoffenberg's personality structure is such that he is willing, more than the average person, to manipulate the truth to his advantage."
Sweet said sentencing would occur the week of Dec. 9.
Hoffenberg, who gained national attention when he offered to rescue the New York Post newspaper in January, 1993, pleaded guilty to the conspiracy and fraud charges in April, 1995.

The flashy financier is accused of being the mastermind of one of the largest so-called Ponzi schemes ever recorded. He sold more than $450 million in fraudulent notes and bonds to investors and used some of the money he collected from later investors to pay interest owed to the earlier ones.
The rest of the money was used to run the Post and to operate his financial empire with inflated revenues and bogus profits that made it appear to be a major health care financing company.
Towers, a bill-collection business, filed for bankruptcy in March 1993.

Although the judge had questioned Hoffenberg during the 1995 plea hearing about whether he was under a doctor's care and what type of medical treatment he was receiving, Hoffenberg argued that the court should have probed further.

Hoffenberg said during the plea hearing that he was being treated for anxiety but had not taken any drugs in the last 24 hours. He argued that Sweet should have questioned him further about his anxiety and about the drugs he was taking.

Sweet found that his questioning had satisfied federal rules governing such inquiries. Doctors' reports concluded that Hoffenberg was depressed the day of the plea hearing, but there was no evidence that his functioning was impaired by his mental state or the drugs he was taking.

Hoffenberg was arrested in February of this year in Little Rock, Ark. after failing to meet new bail terms that had been set a few days earlier. While in Little Rock he said he was planning to run for U.S. Senate.
